title: Families of 55 missing Malaysians in Nepal want moratorium to ease loans, insurance claims - Malay Mail
description: Families of 55 missing Malaysians in Nepal want moratorium to ease loans, insurance claims  Malay Mail
publisher.title: Malay Mail
full_article:
PUTRAJAYA, Sept 27 — Families of 55 Malaysians still missing following the flash flood in Nepal have urged the government to consider a special moratorium on the victims’ financial commitments, as their families are now facing difficulties accessing the victims’ accounts and assets, insurance coverage, and managing their loans.

Malaysia Solidarity: Families in Hope (MASFIH) spokesperson Dr Manivannan Rethinam said that after 33 days without certainty, financial and legal issues have become among the most pressing concerns for the families, particularly as some of the victims were the main breadwinners.

He explained that the moratorium requested was not for all family members but specifically for financial commitments involving the 55 individuals who remain missing.

“We do not need to wait for the Nepalese government. There are many things we can do in Malaysia now. What we are asking for is a special moratorium for the 55 missing individuals, covering all financial commitments under their names or related to them.

googletag.cmd.push(function() {googletag.display("mm-story-mreg-2");});

“This will help the families cope until death certificates are issued and insurance claims and estate matters can be settled,” he told reporters after attending a more than four-hour meeting between the next of kin and government agencies at Wisma Putra here today, involving about 105 people.

googletag.cmd.push(function() {googletag.display("mm-teads");});

The session, which began at about 10.15 am and ended around 3 pm, included briefings on search and rescue (SAR) operations, the management of deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) samples, as well as legal and documentation processes involving the individuals who remain missing.

Manivannan said the victims’ status as missing persons had placed various constraints on their families, as assets and financial commitments under their names could not be managed as usual.

googletag.cmd.push(function() {googletag.display("mm-story-mreg-4");});

These included bank accounts, vehicle and housing loans, company interests, and life and travel insurance claims.

He said some families wanted to return their vehicles because they could no longer afford the payments, but faced difficulties because the vehicles were registered in the missing individuals’ names.

As such, MASFIH wants to hold a meeting with Bank Negara Malaysia, the Attorney General’s Chambers (AGC) and relevant agencies to seek a specific mechanism to resolve the issues faced by the families.

Manivannan said the families have also sought a meeting with Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim to enable a comprehensive solution to be coordinated at the highest government level.

He said the families appreciated the Prime Minister’s earlier move to contact his counterpart Balendra Shah regarding efforts to establish a special mechanism to address the issue, but believed that several measures could be implemented in Malaysia without having to wait for a decision by the Nepalese government.

On efforts to identify the victims, Manivannan said the families were informed that the Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM) had obtained 98 DNA samples from next of kin, all of which had been processed by the Department of Chemistry Malaysia as of Sept 24.

He said the process, which normally takes longer, had been expedited to enable matching to be carried out should any bodies be found.

He said three DNA profiles had also been sent to China following information that three of the missing Malaysians had immigration-related records in the Tibet area.

MASFIH, however, urged that the possibility of sending DNA profiles of other members of the same group also be considered if there was evidence that they had been in the area.

According to Manivannan, representatives of the Malaysian Embassy in Beijing had informed them that if families had information indicating that other individuals were also there, the matter could be discussed with the Chinese authorities.

He said the families had also asked PDRM and the Department of Chemistry to reassess whether the DNA samples obtained from each family were sufficient to establish stronger matches.

Manivannan also said the families appreciated the efforts of the relevant teams in explaining the challenges and search operations being conducted in Nepal.

However, the families questioned why the Malaysian team’s operations could not focus on the Rasuwagadhi area near the Nepal-Tibet border, which was believed to be the last known location of some of the missing Malaysians before contact was lost.

According to him, the families were informed that the areas covered by the Malaysian team’s operations were determined based on permission from the Nepalese authorities, while access to certain areas was beyond the control of the SMART team.

He said the families were also informed that there remained a possibility that victims could be found alive if they were in remote areas or villages, although the possibility was considered very slim.

Manivannan said the families were also informed that the Nepalese government was considering ending the SAR phase and moving into the recovery and reconstruction phase, although no date had been set.

At the same time, he said, the Nepalese authorities were working to expedite the DNA matching process, while discussions were also ongoing on documentation mechanisms relating to disaster victims, adding that the families now needed not only information on the search operations but also a clear direction to address the long-term impact. — Bernama

title: Nepal: Fresh avalanche leaves 10 missing, revives Rasuwa trauma - National Herald
description: Nepal: Fresh avalanche leaves 10 missing, revives Rasuwa trauma  National Herald
publisher.title: National Herald
full_article:
Ten climbers and support staff are missing after an avalanche struck the base camp of 7,126-metre Himlung Himal in Nepal’s Manang district

The incident comes weeks after a massive rock-and-ice collapse in Nepal triggered catastrophic flooding that killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing

Scientists have linked the August disaster to warming-driven glacier thinning and permafrost thaw, highlighting growing climate risks in the Himalayas

Ten climbers and support staff are missing after an avalanche struck the base camp of Himlung Himal in Nepal’s Manang district, the latest in a series of disasters to hit the Himalayan nation amid increasingly volatile weather and growing climate risks.

The avalanche struck the base camp of the 7,126-metre peak in the Nar Phu area, burying tents and cutting off contact with 10 people, according to the Expedition Operators Association Nepal. Eight of those missing are associated with Himalayan Holidays Nepal and two with Imagine Nepal.

Ram Krishna Lamichhane, director general of the Department of Tourism, said authorities were monitoring the situation and working to gather details and locate those unaccounted for. Their identities have not yet been established. Persistent rain and snowfall have affected several of Nepal’s mountain districts in recent days, with authorities warning of avalanche and flash-flood risks.

The incident comes barely a month after a far deadlier mountain disaster in Nepal. On 26 August, a massive rock-and-ice collapse on the Langtang Lirung mountain triggered a high-speed debris flood that swept through communities and infrastructure in the Rasuwa district and across the Nepal-China border.

title: Monsoon floods, landslides kill 68 across India, Nepal in 72 hours | Daily Sabah - Daily Sabah
description: Monsoon floods, landslides kill 68 across India, Nepal in 72 hours | Daily Sabah  Daily Sabah
publisher.title: Daily Sabah
full_article:
At least 68 people were killed in northern India and Nepal in the past 72 hours after heavy rain triggered floods and landslides across the region, authorities said Sunday.

In India's most populous state of Uttar Pradesh, 56 people died and more than 1,000 houses were damaged over the past three days, the Relief Commissioner's office said in a statement.

Neighboring Nepal, already reeling from the catastrophic Aug. 26 flood, was hit by new flooding and landslides that killed 12 people since Thursday.

"Since Thursday, 12 people have died in rain-related disasters such as floods and landslides," Shanti Mahat, spokesperson for Nepal's disaster authority said, adding that seven more were missing.

Scientists have warned in recent years of an increase in extreme weather events across South Asia, linking them to rising temperatures and changing climate patterns.

The flooding in Nepal last month, triggered by a glacial mountain collapse on the China-Nepal border, killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing.

Uttar Pradesh, home to more than 240 million people, frequently experiences rain and thunderstorms during the annual monsoon season from June to September.

The Relief Commissioner's office said the latest deaths occurred during a spell of "exceptionally heavy rain" after a "depression over the Bay of Bengal moved inland and intensified rainfall across the region."

The state recorded 66.5 millimeters of rain between Friday and Sunday, compared to the season average of 7.6 millimeters, it added.

The heavy rain caused extensive crop damage, and farmers raised concerns about sowing delays in the upcoming season.

In India's eastern state of Odisha, officials evacuated more than 70,000 people living in low-lying areas after rivers swelled because of heavy downpours, NDTV news network reported.

The rains damaged bridges and culverts, forcing officials to shut down Devkund, a popular tourist spot in the state.

Monsoon disasters are annual occurrences across India following long summers when many parts of the country face water scarcity and drought.

title: Floods, landslides kill 19 in India, Nepal - Pajhwok Afghan News
description: Floods, landslides kill 19 in India, Nepal  Pajhwok Afghan News
publisher.title: Pajhwok Afghan News
full_article:
KABUL (Pajhwok): At least 19 people have been killed and 10 others remain missing after heavy rains, storms, flash floods and landslides hit parts of India and Nepal, a media report said on Sunday.

In India’s Uttar Pradesh state, 15 people were killed and five others injured over the past 48 hours, while 117 houses were damaged, Reuters reported, quoting state authorities.

Officials said heavy rain and storms affected 63 districts, with the state receiving 19 times its normal rainfall in the 24 hours to Saturday.

In Nepal, four people, including three children and a woman, were killed when a landslide buried their house while they were sleeping in Nishi Khola village in Baglung district, officials said.

Meanwhile, 10 Nepali workers were reported missing after an avalanche buried the base camp of the 7,126-metre Himlung Himal in northern Manang district. The workers had been setting up tents for foreign climbers, who were not at the site when the avalanche struck.

Nepali authorities warned of possible flash floods in 49 of the country’s 77 districts as water levels in major rivers and tributaries continued to rise.

Flooding in the Rahuganga River also damaged transmission-line structures and foundations linked to a 40-megawatt hydropower project. A technical team was sent to assess the damage.

Meanwhile, India’s Central Water Commission said conditions at 30 river monitoring stations in seven states were “severe.”

Water levels in several major rivers, including the Ganges, Gandak, Kosi, Bagmati and Narmada, had risen above danger levels.

Floods and landslides also disrupted telecommunications in parts of Nepal after fibre-optic lines and power networks were damaged.

title: Floods and landslides kill 12 across Nepal - The Kathmandu Post
description: Floods and landslides kill 12 across Nepal  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
At least 12 people have died across Nepal in floods and landslides triggered by persistent heavy rain, with six deaths reported in the past 24 hours, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.

Twelve people have died in floods, landslides and heavy rain since September 24, said Shanti Mahat, spokesperson for the disaster management authority.

Seven people are still missing, including one in Palpa, four in Baglung and two in Myagdi, she said.

The authority stepped up preparations after the Meteorological Forecasting Division issued warnings about heavy rainfall and potential hazards, Mahat said. Based on the level of risk, authorities identified areas under red, amber and yellow alerts and deployed teams from local administrations, security agencies and local government for preparedness and rescue operations.

A separate advisory was also issued for tourists and trekkers after forecasts indicated the possibility of heavy snowfall in mountainous areas alongside the rain, she said.

The authority has maintained regular communication with all 77 chief district officers, district police chiefs, heads of local government and other agencies involved in disaster response, Mahat said.

More than 1,100 moved to safety

The authority said several districts, including Nawalpur, Chitwan, Palpa and Parbat, faced heightened risks of flooding, riverbank erosion and landslides.

Some houses were swept away by floods in Parbat. No deaths were reported there, however, because residents of vulnerable settlements were moved to safer areas in time, Mahat said.

More than 1,100 people in the Nawalparasi area have been relocated to safer locations, she said. Rescue operations are continuing in areas affected by floods and landslides.

Two helicopters have been deployed for rescue operations in Myagdi.

The authority said local government, district administration offices and provincial government were coordinating to provide food and other essential supplies to people moved to safety after the disasters.

In Nepal, 40 insured Israeli tourists are receiving assistance after heavy rains, flood threats and bad weather disrupted trekking routes in the Himalayas. This was reported by the Jerusalem Post, citing the situation center of the PassportCard insurance company.

Tourists in several mountain regions

According to PassportCard, 17 travelers are in the Annapurna region, and another 17 are in the Manaslu region, including in Samagaun. Four tourists are in the Tsum Valley near Chumling, while two are in the Everest region.

Four insured tourists require medical assistance. They are planned to be evacuated for treatment as soon as weather conditions allow. The company said that, according to available information, none of these people is in a life-threatening condition. Their families maintain regular contact with the situation center.

More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.

Restrictions on movement

Local authorities overnight warned of flood risks and urged tourists in popular locations and along trekking routes to move to safer places. Nepalese meteorological services also warned travelers against hiking on high-altitude routes due to the threat of floods, landslides, rockfalls, and damage to trails and bridges.

Travel across a significant part of Nepal is severely restricted due to road closures, and trekking in affected areas has been suspended. PassportCard teams are working simultaneously in several locations and assessing the situation in light of the weather and the ability to travel. According to the company's forecast, the bad weather will gradually weaken, but restoring normal transport links in the affected areas may take several days.

full_article:
Kathmandu: Relentless rainfall since Thursday has killed at least 14 people across Nepal, with inundation, flooding and landslides reported from several parts of the country, prompting alerts and warnings.

Early morning today, authorities issued a warning for residents living along the Narayani River in Central Nepal after it crossed the warning level of 9 metres and entered settlements. Highways leading to Chitwan, which serves as a juncture for travel across the nation, also remain blocked, with landslides reported at multiple locations.

At least six people had died in rain-induced disasters from Thursday until Saturday evening, according to the National Disaster Risk Reduction Management Authority (NDRRMA). Four additional people were killed in a landslide incident in Myagdi District on Sunday morning.

“In Annapurna Village Council, four people have been confirmed dead in a landslide,” Bharat Kumar Pun, the Chairperson of the Village Council, confirmed to ANI.

According to the official, landslides at multiple locations have hindered search and rescue operations, while conditions have been deteriorating with the continuous downpour.

Similarly, a landslide in adjoining Baglung District also killed four additional people, a local official confirmed to ANI.

“In Nishikhola Village Council of Baglung District, four people have died after being buried in a landslide. The incident occurred this morning in Ward Number 3, Hardra,” Prem Bahadur Gharti Magar, the Deputy Chairperson of the Village Council, told ANI over the phone.

The Kaligandaki River flowing through the district has also swept away houses and bridges, disconnecting road connectivity.

Security forces have been carrying out evacuations in multiple districts following inundation and the risk of floods, moving thousands of people to safer locations.

The latest disaster in the Himalayan nation comes a month after the tragedy of the Bhotekoshi floods, which so far have claimed over 1,400 lives and left over 6,000 missing.

The flood struck riverside settlements in Rasuwa district on the morning of Aug. 26 (Bhadra 10, 2083), rapidly affecting neighbouring areas including Nuwakot and Dhading.

Infrastructure losses underscore the scale of the event. Eight operating hydropower projects (281 MW) and four under construction (388 MW) were damaged, disrupting 431.1 MW of generation capacity. Major sections of the Galchhi–Betrawati–Rasuwagadhi road and the Prithvi Highway were destroyed or heavily damaged, along with 48 suspension bridges and 31 motorable bridges.

title: Fourteen Missing As Avalanche Hits Himlung Base Camp - Explorersweb »
description: Fourteen Missing As Avalanche Hits Himlung Base Camp  Explorersweb »
publisher.title: Explorersweb »
full_article:
An avalanche has buried the base camp at the foot of Himlung, a 7,000m peak that several outfitters are guiding this fall. Fourteen local workers are missing. Nepal’s mountains are receiving intense snowfall these days, and everyone was urged to stay in villages to remain safe.

“Two of those unaccounted for are from Imagine Nepal, and eight are from Himalayan Holidays Nepal, the Expedition Outfitters Association of Nepal originally told The Kathmandu Post . A later update increased the number of missing to 14. All are Nepalese. The authorities admit that the bad weather is hampering the rescue efforts. Helicopters are grounded, and volunteers on foot have also been unable to reach the camp.

Himlung. Photo: Wikipedia

There are no foreigners yet on Himlung, as the route is not fixed and Nepal’s Department of Tourism has not yet issued any permits. Last week, rope-fixing teams were assigned to prepare the routes on Himlung and Ama Dablam, but with the big storm approaching, it’s unlikely that they had a chance to start. However, local staff could have been setting up and supplying the base camp in advance of visitors.

Details remain sketchy, but an avalanche at base camp height is rare. Himlung (7,126m) lies in the Nar-Phu Valley, near the Tibetan border. The base camp is usually on flat ground, a respectable distance from the mountain flanks. Last year, it lay on completely dry ground. (Check the feature image of this story and a complete ascent video by 8K Expeditions here).

Himlung Base Camp in a snowy fall. Photo: Climbing the Seven Summits/Mike Hamill

Ample warnings

The storm dumped loads of snow on the mountains as expected, forcing climbers and trekkers to retreat. The Manaslu season has been called off, although a handful of climbers and their guides continue to wait in Samagaon or Pokhara for a possible summit chance when the weather settles down. Six climbers also remain at Base Camp on Dhaulagiri, shoveling snow but safe.

Still shocked by last month’s lethal floods, Nepal authorities have made an extra effort to disseminate warnings, information, and alerts about the storm, which originated in the Bay of Bengal last week. The Annapurna Conservation Area closed to visitors for the weekend, and other popular spots have issued warnings urging trekkers and climbers to stay well away from higher passes, avalanche-prone areas, and even rivers and low-lying mountain slopes that may be prone to floods or landslides from the rain at lower altitudes. Yet surprisingly, a significant number of staff evidently remained at Himlung’s base camp.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

Newly popular

The new popularity of Himlung centers around a tourism law currently under debate in Nepal’s parliament. It would make climbing a 7,000m peak in Nepal a prerequisite for foreigners before attempting Everest.

Imagine Nepal markets Himlung as “an ideal peak for climbers who already have experience climbing at elevations of 6,000m and are looking to push their altitude experience to the next level.” The outfitter explained that this season, their team planned an expedition to Manaslu and later, Himlung.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

The current accident recalls a death that occurred on Himlung during a major storm last year. Chin Tark Chan, 49, of Australia, fell ill shortly before reaching the summit of Himlung just as the weather worsened. The bad weather hampered rescue attempts, and issues with the insurance company, which alleged the climber was stranded at 6,800m, above the altitude limit of helicopters. Eventually, the climber was carried down to Camp 3, where he died.

Landslide in the Manaslu Area

The storm has created problems in several mountain areas. Trekkers and climbers in Samagaon, the village leading to Manaslu Base Camp, were jolted by strong tremors and a powerful roar at 3 am on Sunday.

“We rushed out of our rooms, looking for a safe place. We did not know where to go,” Nepalese IFMGA guide Abiral Rai posted on social media. The cause was not an earthquake, but a landslide above a nearby village. There are no victims reported so far, but both locals and visitors ran outside for safety:

Rai, together with a client, is one of the few who still refuse to call off their Manaslu expedition. They have been waiting at Samagaon for the storm front to pass.
